analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators order refunds when interstate natural gas pipelines overcharge their customers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2021 with bipartisan sponsorship and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Natural Gas Act to make it easier for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to order refunds when a natural gas company charges rates that are unjust, unreasonable, or discriminatory. When FERC opens a proceeding, it would have to set a 'refund effective date' (within about five months of the case being filed), and if the rates turn out to be too high, customers could get their money back — with interest — for the months in between, up to fifteen months' worth. If a gas company stalls the case past that window, FERC could go back even further.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers who pay interstate natural gas rates — including utilities and ultimately the homes and businesses that buy gas through them — would get refunds, with interest, if FERC finds they were overcharged. The refund clock starts when the complaint is filed, so overcharges during the months-long review period would no longer be simply kept by the company.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and businesses buying natural gas

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires FERC to establish a refund effective date whenever it opens a rate proceeding, set no earlier than the complaint filing date and no later than five months after it, so refunds can cover the period while the case is pending.

At the end of a proceeding, FERC may order refunds of amounts paid above the just and reasonable rate — up to fifteen months after the refund effective date — and the refunds must be made with interest to the people who paid the rates.

If a proceeding drags past fifteen months because the natural gas company was dilatory, FERC may order refunds for the entire period back to the refund effective date, removing the payoff from slow-walking the case.
FERC must act with the same speed it applies to its most urgent rate cases and, if no decision comes within 180 days, explain why and give its best estimate of when it will decide.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas pipeline companies and other gas companies whose rates are reviewed under the Natural Gas Act would pay back overcharges, with interest, and face more financial uncertainty about rates under review. Any refund liability they cannot absorb would ultimately come out of shareholder returns or show up in future rate requests.

drawbacks.text: Refunds are capped: they can only cover from the refund effective date through fifteen months after it, so customers overcharged before a complaint was filed cannot recover those amounts.

The burden of proof stays on FERC or the complainant to show a rate is unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential — customers do not get their money back simply by alleging high prices.
The bill applies only to rates regulated under the Natural Gas Act, which covers interstate gas companies; most home heating bills are set by state regulators and would not be affected by it.
Backdated refunds with interest add financial uncertainty for pipeline companies while rates are under review, which critics argue can raise their financing costs and, over time, the rates they seek.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is concrete but modest: refunds with interest for overcharges that occur while a case is pending, and less incentive for gas companies to drag out proceedings. The bill does not change how rates are set, does not cover state-regulated retail rates, and still requires FERC or a complainant to prove the rate was improper, so it helps mainly in cases regulators actually bring. The main cost falls on gas companies, though in the long run some of it could be passed into future rates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative G. K. Butterfield, a North Carolina Democrat, introduced the bill on June 17, 2021, joined by Representative Billy Long, a Missouri Republican.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy.
No further action was recorded — no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas companies are better off: no refund mechanism was created, so any past and future overcharges under Natural Gas Act review remain uncollectible the way this bill would have made them recoverable. Ordinary gas customers are left with the existing, weaker refund rules.

for.name: Rep. G. K. Butterfield
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require a refund effective date and order refunds for unjust natural gas rates.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 17, 2021 and never scheduled a markup or vote, sending it to the Subcommittee on Energy where it stayed until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a North Carolina Democrat with one Missouri Republican cosponsor — and no opposition was ever recorded because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have let FERC order refunds, with interest, of rates found unjust or unreasonable during rate review proceedings — up to fifteen months of overcharges, or more if the company slow-walked the case. That takes money back from companies whose rates have historically been presumptively collectible while cases drag on.
Utilities and ultimately the households and businesses they serve could recover overcharges paid on interstate gas rates, with interest, once FERC found the rates improper.
